title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler has derived the equation for the transverse vibration of an elastic lamina (Euler–Bernoulli beam), y_tt = -b^4 y_xxxx. The previous page sets four boundary conditions for a clamped–free blade: at the free end x=0, y_xx=0 and y_xxx=0; at the clamped end x=a, y=0 and y_x=0. He has just admitted that he cannot find a complete integral containing four arbitrary functions, analogous to d'Alembert's solution for the vibrating string.

This page offers a partial substitute. Take four arbitrary functions of time P(t), Q(t), R(t), S(t) as Cauchy data at x=0. Then posit the power series in x/b
y = Σ_n c_n(t) (x/b)^n, with c_0=P, c_1=Q, c_2=R, c_3=S, c_4=P', c_5=Q', and so on.
Next compute -y_tt and b^4 y_xxxx term by term and equate coefficients. This gives
n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)·c_n = -c_{n-4}''(t), i.e.
P' = -P''/(1·2·3·4), Q' = -Q''/(2·3·4·5), and so on.
Iterating, P'' (the eighth coefficient) = +P^{(4)}/8!, and similarly for Q, R, S.
In modern terms, y is the sum of four series:
Σ_k (-1)^k P^{(2k)}(t) x^{4k}/((4k)! b^{4k})
+ Σ_k (-1)^k Q^{(2k)}(t) x^{4k+1}/((4k+1)! b^{4k+1})
+ 2Σ_k (-1)^k R^{(2k)} x^{4k+2}/((4k+2)! b^{4k+2})
+ 6Σ_k (-1)^k S^{(2k)} x^{4k+3}/((4k+3)! b^{4k+3}).
The factors 2 and 6 appear because R and S are not factorial-normalised.

This is a formal solution of the Cauchy problem with data on the line x=0 (non-characteristic). It is the beam-equation analogue of the familiar heat-equation series Σ f^{(k)}(t) x^{2k}/(2k)!. Each of the four series separately solves the PDE, which Euler notes on the next page. He then remarks that this gains little for the actual problem, because the boundary conditions at x=a cannot be imposed usefully this way. He therefore turns to separated solutions cos(θ²t)(A cos θx/b + B sin θx/b + C e^{θx/b} + D e^{-θx/b}).

Correctness: the recursion is right. The series converges, entire in x, e.g. for P analytic in t, and more generally when P^{(2k)} = O(C^k (4k)!^{1-ε}).
errors: The printed formulas for P'', Q'', R'', S'' have dt^2 in the denominator; it should be dt^4, since these are fourth time derivatives.
In the series for b^4 y_xxxx, the R'' term is printed as b^6/x^6; it should be x^6/b^6.
On the following page the leading terms are written Qx, Rx^2, Sx^3 without the factors 1/b, 1/b^2, 1/b^3, which is inconsistent with the ansatz. The d^6 terms also have dt^2 for dt^6.
On the following page the sign of the x^15 d^6S term is printed + but should be − (alternating pattern).

ideas.what: Power-series solution of y_tt = -b^4 y_xxxx in the space variable, with four arbitrary time functions as data at x=0, giving four independent series solutions
ideas.modern_name: Formal Cauchy (Cauchy–Kovalevskaya-type) series solution with data on a non-characteristic line; analogue of the heat-equation series Σ f^{(k)}(t)x^{2k}/(2k)!
ideas.usually_credited_to: General theory: Cauchy (1842) and Kovalevskaya (1875). Heat-equation series and Gevrey/uniqueness issues: Holmgren, Tychonoff, Widder (20th c.). Closed-form beam solution via Fresnel-type integrals: Poisson/Boussinesq (19th c.)
ideas.where_published: E443 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 17, 1772/73); discussed in Truesdell's 1960 history of elastic bodies (Opera omnia II.11 part 2)

ideas.what: Admission that no complete integral with four arbitrary functions (d'Alembert-type) is known for the beam equation
ideas.modern_name: Absence of a d'Alembert-type general solution for a dispersive equation; later integral representations via factorisation into Schrödinger-type operators
ideas.where_published: E443, §XI; also Euler's earlier lamina papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine formal power-series solution and a known admission of failure. It is well documented in Truesdell's account of Euler's elastic-vibration work. Euler draws no convergence or uniqueness insight from it, so it is not an anticipation of later results.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the printed 'R'' b^6/x^6'; this is a printing error for x^6/b^6, not a transcription error.
The P'' line reads 'P'' = -ddP'/(5.6.7.8 dt^2) = +d^4P/(1.2.3.4.5.6.7.8 dt^2)'. The printed dt^2 in the d^4 expressions (also in Q'', R'', S'') should mathematically be dt^4.
